claim: Adult zebrafish exhibit a striking striped pattern generated through the self-organisation of three different chromatophores.
source: Adult zebrafish exhibit a striking striped pattern generated through the self-organisation of three different chromatophores.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is a well-established observation about zebrafish pigment patterns.

claim: The model qualitatively and quantitatively reproduces wild type and mutant pigment pattern development.
source: The model qualitatively and quantitatively reproduces wild type and mutant pigment pattern development.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results presented throughout the manuscript, including Figures 5-7 showing qualitative matches and Figure 10 showing quantitative comparisons.

claim: Zebrafish generate a robust adult stripe pattern of alternating dark blue stripes and golden interstripes comprised of three different pigment-producing cell types: melanocytes, xanthophores, and iridophores.
source: Zebrafish generate, over a period of a few weeks and beginning around 3 weeks of age (Frohnhöfer et al., 2013; Parichy et al., 2009), a robust adult stripe pattern of alternating dark blue stripes and golden interstripes comprised of three different pigment-producing cell types: melanocytes, containing black melanin; xanthophores containing yellow and orange carotenoids and pteridines; and iridescent iridophores, containing guanine crystals within reflective platelets (Hirata et al., 2003; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published experimental work (Frohnhöfer et al., 2013; Parichy et al., 2009; Hirata et al., 2003) and Figure 1A.

claim: There are two types of S-iridophores distinguished by their platelet distribution: type L-iridophores and type S-iridophores.
source: Of the iridophores, there are two types distinguished by their platelet distribution (Hirata et al., 2003); type L-iridophores, and type S-iridophores.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hirata et al., 2003.

claim: Only type S-iridophores play a role in stripe formation.
source: Only type S-iridophores play a role in stripe formation (type L-iridophores appear later and are likely involved in pattern maintenance [Hirata et al., 2003])
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hirata et al., 2003.

claim: S-iridophores appear in two different forms: dense S-iridophores in light interstripes and loose S-iridophores in dark stripes.
source: In the light interstripes, S-iridophores appear in a 'dense' arrangement (dense S-iridophores), forming a continuous sheet, whilst in the dark stripes the cells are in a 'loose' arrangement and appear more widely spaced (loose S-iridophores) (Hirata et al., 2003; Fadeev et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hirata et al., 2003 and Fadeev et al., 2015.

claim: Adult dark stripes consist of consecutive layers of L-iridophores, melanocytes, loose S-iridophores and xanthophores.
source: Starting from the deepest layer of the hypodermis just above the muscle and moving to the dermis, adult dark stripes consist of consecutive layers of L-iridophores, melanocytes, loose S-iridophores and xanthophores.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hirata et al., 2003 and Figure 1B.

claim: Adult light interstripes are made up of layers of dense S-iridophores and xanthophores.
source: Similarly, adult light interstripes are made up of layers of dense S-iridophores and xanthophores (Figure 1B; Hirata et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hirata et al., 2003 and Figure 1B.

claim: Early larval xanthophores dedifferentiate, forming unpigmented xanthoblasts that regain their proliferative ability and proceed to generate the adult xanthophores.
source: Early larval xanthophores dedifferentiate, forming unpigmented xanthoblasts that regain their proliferative ability and proceed to generate the adult xanthophores (McMenamin et al., 2014; Mahalwar et al., 2014; Parichy et al., 2000b)
evidence: This is supported by citations to McMenamin et al., 2014; Mahalwar et al., 2014; Parichy et al., 2000b.

claim: Xanthophore de-differentiation is complete by 21dpf.
source: Xanthophore de-differentiation is complete by 21dpf, and early metamorphic melanocytes appear in a widely scattered distribution between 14 and 21dpf (Parichy et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Parichy et al., 2009.

claim: Early metamorphic melanocytes appear in a widely scattered distribution between 14 and 21dpf.
source: Xanthophore de-differentiation is complete by 21dpf, and early metamorphic melanocytes appear in a widely scattered distribution between 14 and 21dpf (Parichy et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Parichy et al., 2009.

claim: A key event in the initiation of adult pattern metamorphosis is the appearance of newly differentiated dense S-iridophores alongside the horizontal myoseptum.
source: A key event in the initiation of adult pattern metamorphosis is the appearance of newly differentiated dense S-iridophores alongside the horizontal myoseptum.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the description of pattern development.

claim: The first adult xanthophores are generated by differentiation from xanthoblasts in response to the appearance of dense S-iridophores.
source: In response to the appearance of these S-iridophores, the first adult xanthophores are generated (Figure 1C, stage PR) by differentiation from xanthoblasts in this region, thus initiating the first interstripe, X0.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: S-iridophores proliferate rapidly and spread bidirectionally after their initial appearance.
source: Subsequently, S-iridophores proliferate rapidly and spread bidirectionally; at the edges of the interstripes they switch to a more scattered (less tightly-packed) form as they continue to spread dorsally and ventrally.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing pattern development.

claim: Spreading loose S-iridophores transition back into dense S-iridophores at the locations of future interstripes.
source: Spreading loose S-iridophores transition back into dense S-iridophores at the locations of the future interstripes X1V and X1D (Figure 1C, stages PR to SP) (Mahalwar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mahalwar et al., 2014 and Figure 1C.

claim: Without any one of the three pigment cell types (melanocytes, xanthophores, S-iridophores), pattern formation is disrupted.
source: The pattern is formed by cell–cell interactions of all three pigment producing cell types: melanocytes, xanthophores and S-iridophores. Without any one of these cell types, pattern formation is disrupted (Frohnhöfer et al., 2013; Patterson and Parichy, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Frohnhöfer et al., 2013 and Patterson and Parichy, 2013.

claim: Previous mathematical models of zebrafish stripe formation have not incorporated S-iridophores.
source: Until the last few years, these studies have focused on melanocytes and xanthophores, neglecting S-iridophores.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: Without S-iridophores, spots of melanocyte aggregates form instead of stripes.
source: In particular, it has been shown that without S-iridophores, spots of melanocyte aggregates form instead of stripes, which is contrary to what these Turing reaction-diffusion models predict.
evidence: This is stated in the text and refers to experimental observations.

claim: The model is built as an agent-based model incorporating all three pigment cell-types and their documented cellular interactions.
source: In particular, we construct an agent-based model incorporating all three pigment cell-types and their documented cellular interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the modeling approach.

claim: The model correctly predicts the patterns observed in vivo for wild type and mutant fish.
source: We show that in each case our model correctly predicts the patterns observed in vivo, and that pattern development displays multiple quantitative matches to that in vivo using a parameter sampling methodology to demonstrate the robustness of these patterns to parameter variation.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results presented in Figures 5-7 and quantitative comparisons in Figure 10.

claim: The model demonstrates that current biological understanding is sufficient to explain adult pigment pattern formation in WT and multiple mutants.
source: Our work demonstrates that current biological understanding, alongside simple assumptions about S-iridophore behaviour, is sufficient to explain adult pigment pattern formation in WT and multiple mutants.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the successful simulation of multiple phenotypes.

claim: The model does not directly model L-iridophores since these appear after the adult pattern is formed.
source: We do not directly model L-iridophores, since these appear after the adult pattern is formed and are more likely involved in pattern maintenance (Frohnhöfer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citation to Frohnhöfer et al., 2013.

claim: The model includes xanthoblasts as an independent cell-type because larval xanthoblasts appear principally by dedifferentiation of embryonic xanthophores.
source: Unlike previous models of stripe formation (Nakamasu et al., 2009; Bullara and De Decker, 2015; Volkening and Sandstede, 2015; Painter et al., 2015; Bloomfield et al., 2011; Volkening and Sandstede, 2018), we include xanthoblasts as an independent cell-type in our model. This is because the larval xanthoblasts appear principally by dedifferentiation of the embryonic xanthophores, and most metamorphic xanthophores arise from the larval xanthoblasts (Mahalwar et al., 2014; McMenamin et al., 2014; Budi et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2014; Dooley et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Each of the three pigment cell layers is modeled as an independent, two-dimensional lattice domain.
source: For consistency, we model each of the three layers as independent, two-dimensional lattice domains throughout pattern formation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Lattice sites within the xanthophore and S-iridophore model layers are half the width and length of melanocyte sites.
source: To account for the different packing densities of the cell types, lattice sites within the xanthophore and S-iridophore model layers are half the width and length of melanocyte sites size.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The domain height is set to 1 mm, which is the approximate height of the fish at 25 dpf.
source: We set the domain height to be 1 mm, since this is the approximate height of the fish at 25 dpf (Supplementary file 3 for details)
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by Supplementary file 3.

claim: The domain length is set to 2 mm, representing approximately one-third of the full length at 25 dpf.
source: we set the domain length to be 2 mm, representing approximately one-third of the full length, from the tip of the snout to the start of the tail, at 25 dpf, and thus equivalent to the trunk (Parichy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citation to Parichy et al., 2009.

claim: The model is updated according to the Gillespie algorithm.
source: The model is then updated according to the Gillespie algorithm (Gillespie, 1977).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citation to Gillespie, 1977.

claim: The model includes uniform domain growth with rate 0.13 mm per day in horizontal axis and 0.033 mm per day in the vertical axis.
source: Events incorporated into our model include all processes involved in the self-organisation of pigment cells during pattern metamorphosis as well as uniform domain growth with rate 0.13 mm per day in horizontal axis and 0.033 mm per day in the vertical axis (Parichy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citation to Parichy et al., 2009.

claim: Cells interact at both short range (neighboring cells) and long range (up to half a stripe width ≈0.25 mm).
source: Cells interact in the fish skin at both short (neighbouring cells) and long (up to half a stripe width ≈0.25 mm) range, with interactions thought to use direct contact through cellular extensions (filopodia, dendrites, or longer airenemes).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Uniform disks with radii on the order of the distance between 2 cells (≈0.04 mm) account for short-range interactions in the model.
source: In our model, uniform disks, with radii on the order of the distance between 2 cells (≈0.04 mm) account for short-range interactions (Figure 3A–D)
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: An annulus with an outer radius of 0.24 mm and inner radius of 0.22 mm represents long-range dynamics in the model.
source: and an annulus with an outer radius of 0.24 mm (12 cells) and inner radius of 0.22 mm, (11 cells) represent long-range dynamics (Figure 3E–H).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and shown in Figure 3E-H.

claim: Dense S-iridophores show a directional bias towards xanthophores in the short range.
source: We further predict that dense S-iridophores show a directional bias towards xanthophores in the short range.
evidence: This is a prediction made by the authors based on observations of mutants.

claim: Dense S-iridophores are attracted to xanthophores because they are highly associated with each other in mutants and WT.
source: We propose that dense S-iridophores are attracted in the short range to xanthophores since they are highly associated with each other in each of the mutants and in WT (Frohnhöfer et al., 2013), and this mutual attraction may be important for interstripe consolidation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors and supported by citation to Frohnhöfer et al., 2013.

claim: Loose S-iridophores show a directional bias away from other loose S-iridophores in the short range.
source: Furthermore, loose S-iridophores show a directional bias away from other loose S-iridophores in the short range.
evidence: This is a prediction made by the authors.

claim: Loose S-iridophores are repelled by other loose S-iridophores to facilitate prompt spreading across stripe regions.
source: We propose that loose S-iridophores are repelled by other loose S-iridophores as this would facilitate the prompt spreading of loose S-iridophores across the stripe regions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: S-iridophores spread by proliferation of existing cells (between once and twice per day) combined with quick migration.
source: It has been shown using clonal cell analysis that during pattern metamorphosis S-iridophores spread across the skin of the zebrafish bidirectionally by proliferation of existing cells (between once and twice per day) combined with quick migration (Mahalwar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mahalwar et al., 2014.

claim: The transition between loose and dense S-iridophore forms appears to be interchangeable.
source: The transition between the two types appears to be interchangeable.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing S-iridophore behavior.

claim: Dense S-iridophores can change to loose type when they spread beyond the boundary of the first X0 interstripe.
source: When dense S-iridophores initially spread beyond the boundary of the first X0 interstripe, they can later change to loose type (Fadeev et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fadeev et al., 2015.

claim: Loose S-iridophores can aggregate and form dense S-iridophores when they reach an interstripe region.
source: Similarly when loose S-iridophores reach an interstripe region, they can aggregate and form dense S-iridophores.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing S-iridophore behavior.

claim: Loss of Tjp1a function in sbr mutants compromises the transition of S-iridophores from dense to loose state.
source: It has, however, been shown that loss of Tjp1a function in sbr mutants compromises the transition of S-iridophores from dense to loose state, suggesting that Tjp1a contributes to regulation of the molecular switch that regulates S-iridophore shape changes during their dispersal (Fadeev et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fadeev et al., 2015.

claim: The model simulations reproduce qualitatively most aspects of the biological pattern for wild type fish.
source: The simulations reproduce qualitatively most aspects of the biological pattern.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5A'-D' showing simulation results.

claim: In 100 simulations, 100% of shd stage J+ mutants observed two pseudo-stripes (1D and 1V).
source: We found that in 100 simulations, 100% of shd stage J+ mutants observed two pseudo-stripes (1D and 1V) just as in Figure 5H.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing simulation outcomes.

claim: The mean of widest spot width over one hundred shd simulations was 0.18 of the simulated length.
source: We found that on the average, the mean of widest spot width over one hundred simulations was 0.18 of the simulated length.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing quantitative analysis of shd simulations.

claim: In one hundred pfe simulations, the median number of pseudo-stripes at stage J+ was four, as in WT.
source: In one hundred simulations, the median number of pseudo-stripes at stage J+ in these repeats was four, as WT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pfe simulation outcomes.

claim: In one hundred pfe simulations, the average longest stretch of melanophores was 0.6 of the full length.
source: For example, in one hundred simulations, the average longest stretch of melanophores in any given simulation was 0.6 of the full length.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pfe simulation outcomes.

claim: Small perturbations to the rate parameters still generate consistent patterning in WT and mutant simulations, demonstrating the robustness of the model.
source: We observe for all one hundred repeats and in all three mutants, that small perturbations to the rate parameters still generate consistent patterning, demonstrating the robustness of the model.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6 and Appendix 4—figure 1.

claim: The model successfully replicates the patterns of rse, sbr, and cho mutants.
source: We showed in Figure 7K'–N' that our model could replicate the sbr pattern development by altering the rate at which S-iridophores attempt to change from loose to dense to be slower than in WT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7.

claim: The model successfully simulates regeneration patterns after ablation experiments.
source: In both cases, our simulations closely approximate the published observations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing regeneration simulations and supported by Figures 8 and 9.

claim: The simulated data for melanocyte numbers falls within the error bars of the measured data in real fish at all stages except stage SP.
source: Moreover, in all stages, except for stage SP, the simulated data falls within the error bars of the measured data in real fish.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The real J+ mutant X0 interstripe widths fall in the range of ±1 standard deviations of the simulated J+ X0 stripe width averaged over 100 simulations.
source: We demonstrate in Figure 5B that, in all cases, the real J+ mutant X0 interstripe widths fall in the range of ±1 standard deviations of the simulated J+ X0 stripe width averaged over 100 simulations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10B.

claim: In the model simulations, there is a mean of 4.01 times as many xanthophores in the interstripes than melanocytes in the stripes.
source: In our model simulations, we observe a mean of 4.01 times as many xanthophores in the interstripes than melanocytes in the stripes demonstrating good agreement.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pigment cell density.

claim: All interactions involving S-iridophore transitions are necessary for pattern formation in WT and single cell mutants nac and pfe.
source: To summarise, all interactions are necessary for pattern formation in WT and single cell mutants, nac and pfe.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 11.

claim: Increased height-to-length ratio is correlated with stripes becoming more tortuous in simulations.
source: Interestingly, we also observed in our simulations that increased height-to-length ratio is correlated with stripes becoming more tortuous (R = −0.617, p<0.01, Figure 14C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 14C.

claim: The model predicts that S-iridophores play a more important role in melanocyte differentiation than xanthophores.
source: Our model is the first, to the best of our knowledge, to suggest that S-iridophores play a more important role in melanocyte differentiation than xanthophores.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by simulation results.

claim: The model proposes five hypotheses about cell-cell interactions affected by the leo gene.
source: Then, in a systematic approach we deduced four hypotheses about cell–cell interactions that might be affected by leo, which, upon implementing in our model, successfully replicated the patterns observed in leo, leo;pfe, leo;nac, leo;shd and leo;sbr.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 15.

claim: The model suggests that melanocyte repulsion from xanthophores may not be necessary to generate the characteristic leo spots.
source: This suggests that the cell–cell interaction mediating repulsion of melanocytes by xanthophores in leo, may not be necessary to generate the characteristic spots.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 15F.

claim: The model predicts that the leo;sbr double mutant would display more elongated spots than leo mutants.
source: Comparison with our simulation of leo (Figure 15H') demonstrates that our simulation of leo;sbr also displays more elongated spots than those of our leo simulations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 15L'.

claim: The model predicts that initial S-iridophore interstripe orientation alone does not determine the orientation of stripes and interstripes.
source: Interestingly, instead of observing vertical bars, at stage J+ we observe a labyrinthine pattern. This demonstrates that, whilst the initial S-iridophore interstripe plays a role in orientating the pattern, it is not the only part of the initial condition that is important.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 13A.

claim: The position of the initial S-iridophore interstripe is important for successful pattern formation.
source: We observe that subsequent stripes and interstripes still appear sequentially, either side of the initial interstripe, suggesting that the S-iridophores do play a role in the positioning of new stripes and interstripes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 13B.

claim: Initial domain size contributes to the number of stripes and interstripes.
source: This suggests that the initial domain height influences the number of stripes and interstripes that develop, provided that growth is uniform and centred.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 13C.

claim: Stripe insertion can occur on an initially striped domain in the model.
source: We observe that, in this case, new interstripes do appear between pre-established stripes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 13D.

claim: The model reinforces the growing realization that S-iridophores are crucial for stripe formation.
source: Our work reinforces the growing realisation in the field that the previously neglected S-iridophores are crucial for stripe formation, suggests a minimum set of their rules, and reveals unexpected subtleties to the phenotypic impact of the well-studied leo mutant.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section as a conclusion of the work.

claim: The model reveals unexpected subtleties to the phenotypic impact of the leo mutant.
source: Our work reinforces the growing realisation in the field that the previously neglected S-iridophores are crucial for stripe formation, suggests a minimum set of their rules, and reveals unexpected subtleties to the phenotypic impact of the well-studied leo mutant.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section as a conclusion of the work.

claim: The model is the first to demonstrate the impact of the sbr mutation on pattern formation.
source: This paper represents the first demonstration, to the best of our knowledge, of a model being used explicitly to test the impact of the sbr mutation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The sbr gene encodes Tjp1a, a key tight junction protein expressed at higher levels in dense S-iridophores than loose S-iridophores.
source: The sbr gene encodes Tjp1a, a key tight junction protein, and is expressed at much higher levels in S-iridophores in a dense configuration than those of the loose form (Fadeev et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation to Fadeev et al., 2015.

claim: In sbr mutants, the transition from dense to loose S-iridophores is delayed.
source: These authors also show that in sbr mutants the transition from dense to loose S-iridophores is delayed, suggesting that this transition somehow depends upon Tjp1a in dense S-iridophores (Fadeev et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation to Fadeev et al., 2015.

claim: The model provides theoretical support for the deduction that S-iridophore state transition depends on Tjp1a.
source: This provides theoretical support for Fadeev and colleagues deductions and deepens the interest in understanding the mechanistic basis for this role for Tjp1a.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Growth is important for determining the final pattern in addition to the initial condition.
source: Careful observations of our simulations indicate that in addition to the initial condition, growth is important for determining the final pattern.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on simulation results.

claim: The model can replicate a different stripe formation mechanism seen in Pomocanthus fish.
source: Finally, by initialising a domain that is already populated with cells in a stripe position that we can replicate a different stripe formation mechanism seen in fish Pomocanthus.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 13D.

claim: A stronger signaling capacity of S-iridophores than xanthophores for long range melanocyte differentiation results in better qualitative and quantitative match for shd and pfe mutant patterns.
source: We found that by implementing a stronger signaling capacity of S-iridophores than xanthophores for long range melanocyte differentiation then we obtained a better qualitative and quantitative match for shd and pfe mutant patterns.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by simulation results.

claim: The model reinforces findings that S-iridophores play an important role in determining stripe and interstripe width.
source: Thus, our study further reinforces findings that S-iridophores play an important role in determining stripe and interstripe width (without S-iridophores, X0 interstripe width in shd is increased) and not just the widely reported role of stripe alignment.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on simulation results.

claim: The leo gene encodes Connexin 39.4, which is required in melanocytes and xanthophores but not S-iridophores.
source: The gene leo encodes Connexin 39.4, which is required in melanocytes and xanthophores but not S-iridophores (Irion et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation to Irion et al., 2014.

claim: Leo melanocytes are not repelled by xanthophores in the short range, unlike WT melanocytes.
source: This study by demonstrated that unlike WT melanocytes, leo melanocytes are not repelled by xanthophores in the short range (Yamanaka and Kondo, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation to Yamanaka and Kondo, 2014.

claim: The model provides testable hypotheses about the effect of leo which can guide future experimental work.
source: This work provides testable hypotheses about the effect of leo which can now guide future experimental work.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The rules proposed for zebrafish pigment patterns are complex and extensive compared to most previous mathematical studies.
source: In contrast to most previous mathematical studies of pattern formation, the rules we propose for zebrafish pigment patterns are complex and extensive.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Small parameter changes in the model do not typically generate qualitatively different patterns, unlike Turing reaction-diffusion models.
source: A major difference between our model and Turing reaction-diffusion models is that small parameter changes in our model do not typically generate qualitatively different patterns, whereas Turing reaction-diffusion models can show substantial pattern changes in response to small alterations to parameters near to bifurcation points (Watanabe and Kondo, 2015; Maini et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: The added complexity of the real system has evolved to make the patterning process robust, with partially redundant mechanisms insulating against stochastic variation.
source: We suggest that the added complexity of the real system has evolved to make the patterning process robust, with partially redundant mechanisms insulating against the impact of stochastic variation during pattern formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: The modeling approach is analogous to that adopted by Volkening and Sandstede, 2018.
source: Our modelling approach is analogous to that adopted in another recent study of zebrafish pattern formation, one which independently attempts to understand S-iridophore contributions to the process (Volkening and Sandstede, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation to Volkening and Sandstede, 2018.

claim: The model uses an on-lattice approach while Volkening et al. use an off-lattice model.
source: First, we use an on-lattice model, whilst Volkening et al use an off-lattice model.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section comparing the two modeling approaches.

claim: The model uses a continuous-time method while Volkening et al. update their model at simulated 24 hr intervals.
source: Secondly, we used a continuous-time model, whereas Volkening et al update their model at simulated 24 hr intervals, with all rules implemented simultaneously.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section comparing the two modeling approaches.

claim: The model incorporates a hypothesis that S-iridophores contribute more strongly to promoting melanocyte differentiation than xanthophores.
source: Finally, we incorporate a hypothesis that S-iridophores contribute more strongly to promoting melanocyte differentiation than xanthophore differentiation, leading us to a better qualitative approximation of shd mutants and a better quantitative estimate of melanocyte numbers in shd, pfe and rse than shown before.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section comparing the two modeling approaches.

claim: The independent mathematical approaches of this study and Volkening et al. are mutually reinforcing in concluding that the deduced biological rules may be largely sufficient to explain pigment pattern formation.
source: More broadly, we consider that our independent mathematical approaches are mutually reinforcing in reaching the conclusion that the deduced biological rules may be largely sufficient to explain pigment pattern formation in zebrafish.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: In pfe mutants, melanocyte numbers drop from approximately 90% of WT at stage J+ to approximately 50% by adulthood.
source: Work by Frohnhöfer et al., 2013 has demonstrated that in pfe mutants, which up to stage J+ have similar numbers of melanocytes to WTs (approximately 90% of WT numbers), this drops to approximately 50% of WT by adulthood.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation to Frohnhöfer et al., 2013.

claim: Preliminary simulations up to adulthood suggest the sharp decrease in melanocyte numbers in pfe is not predicted by the current model.
source: Whilst our model correctly predicts melanocyte numbers in pfe compared to WT prior to J+, preliminary simulations up to adulthood suggest this sharp decrease in melanocyte numbers shown in real fish are currently not predicted by our model.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: New biological mechanisms concerning maintenance, likely involving late differentiating L-iridophores, need to be analyzed and incorporated into a model extending to later developmental stages.
source: This clearly indicates that new biological mechanisms concerning maintenance, likely involving the late differentiating L-iridophores, need to be analysed and incorporated into a model that extends to these later developmental stages.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a future direction.

claim: The on-lattice model is amenable to the derivation of a continuum model.
source: From an analytical perspective, an advantage of our on-lattice model is its amenability to the derivation of a continuum model, although we note that continuum approximations to off-lattice individual-based models can also be derived.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The model opens up the opportunity for future exploratory work using a continuum model for mutants pfe and nac.
source: Our model therefore opens up the opportunity for future exploratory work using a continuum model for mutants pfe and nac in order to explore whether pattern formation in these cases individually can be described as Turing patterns and to determine parameter ranges for successful pattern formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a future direction.

claim: The model predicts that mechanisms preserving pattern integrity in fish with particular height to length bias may be related to the position of growth.
source: We predict that this may be related to the position of growth. Thus, future work will be to fully evaluate the effects of growth on the final pattern formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a prediction and future direction.

claim: Agouti is a key regulator of dorso-ventral countershading in zebrafish pigment patterns.
source: We have recently noted the subtle impact of dorso-ventral countershading on the WT zebrafish pigment pattern, including in the stripes themselves, and have identified Agouti as a key regulator of this process (Cal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation to Cal et al., 2019.

claim: The model will allow exploration of possible drivers of dorso-ventral asymmetry in pigment patterns.
source: Our model will allow us to explore possible drivers of this asymmetry, which we hypothesise will include Agouti signalling and also differential domain growth.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a future direction.

claim: The model highlights areas where knowledge is currently incomplete.
source: Our model also highlights areas where knowledge is currently incomplete and, importantly, has allowed in silico investigations to identify plausible mechanisms that require experimental testing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion.
